title: The School of Life
alternate_titles: The School of Life: An Emotional Education

contents: Introduction: the case for an emotional education
Self: self-knowledge, the influence of childhood, philosophical meditation
Others: charity of interpretation, politeness, vulnerability
Relationships: against romanticism; love as a skill rather than an emotion
Work: meaning, career anxieties, and the consolations of realistic ambition
Culture: art, ritual, and ideas as therapeutic resources

audiences: Readers who want a humane, literary introduction to emotional intelligence
People navigating love and relationship disappointments
Fans of The School of Life's videos and classes
Readers of philosophy who want it aimed at daily life

sources.title: Emotional intelligence: an integrative meta-analysis and cascading model
sources.author_or_publisher: Joseph and Newman; Journal of Applied Psychology
sources.supports: External calibration: emotional intelligence is not one settled construct; ability and mixed measures overlap differently with cognitive ability and personality and relate differently to performance.
sources.limitations: Work-performance meta-analysis, not a direct test of the book's humanistic curriculum.

sources.title: The Impact of Enhancing Students' Social and Emotional Learning
sources.author_or_publisher: Durlak et al.; Child Development; indexed by the US Office of Justice Programs
sources.supports: External calibration: structured, implemented social and emotional learning programmes can improve skills, attitudes, behaviour, and academic outcomes.
sources.limitations: School-based programmes for children; it supports teachability in a neighbouring domain, not this essay collection's effectiveness.
